newsitem.title: USA: Yeltsin health doubts mar Russia's G7 success.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin health doubts mar Russia's G7 success.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin began the Group of Seven summit in triumph, but his failure to attend a gala concert revived questions about the health of the man hailed as the guarantor of Russia's reforms.

Yeltsin's aides, suddenly on the defensive again, said he skipped the concert on Saturday because he was tired after two days at the summit, where he was feted by world leaders and celebrated by blowing kisses to eager crowds.

The 66-year-old president's clear speech and firm gait when he resurfaced for Sunday's final session dispelled the worst fears. But his appearance failed to remove all concerns that his health is fragile seven months after he had heart surgery.

"It is obvious that after the hard work of the two days, plus the altitude and the heat, the president required some extra rest," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said, fielding one question after another about Yeltsin's health.
Russian reform chief Anatoly Chubais said the president had simply been "a little bit tired".

The G7 leaders' treatment of Yeltsin, who returned to the Kremlin last February after eight months out with heart trouble and then pneumonia, underlined just how important they think he is for stability in Russia. He has no obvious successor.
A French official said Yeltsin and his delegation had "inspired confidence in everybody". Before the summit, a Russian official said: "It is hard to separate Yeltsin and the new Russia."
Until Saturday night, Yeltsin had plenty to celebrate in Denver, playing a bigger role than at previous G7 summits and being excluded from only one session, on economic issues.

The leaders of the seven industrial countries let him bask in the limelight as a reward for his role as standard-bearer of reforms and for signing a partnership deal with NATO in May, despite opposing the alliance's expansion into eastern Europe.

A major success for Russia was the announcement of an agreement to let it join the Paris Club of creditor nations, which Chubais said would clear the way to Russia winning a better credit rating for its own debt.

Yeltsin said he expected Russia to be allowed to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO) this year and hoped for an agreement this summer to revise a 1990 treaty on conventional arms which Moscow says is outdated.
Russia also agreed during the summit to hold annual meetings with Japan and made the symbolic gesture of promising to stop pointing its missiles at Japan.
Yeltsin, like the G7 leaders, hailed the summit as evidence of Russia's economic progress and confirmation of its role as an important world power.
"The G8 already exists," Yeltsin declared, referring to the G7 as if Russia already had full membership.
But there were also disappointments for Russia. Despite Yeltsin's bravado, the G7 did not become the G8 and France and Japan, in particular, said they were wary of admitting Russia.
There was no announcement of major progress towards another Russian aim -- joining the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.

The improvement in ties with Japan left unsolved the main problem dogging relations -- a dispute over ownership of four Pacific islands which Yastrzhembsky said was unlikely to be resolved this generation.
Despite the mutual backslapping which dominated the summit, Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov issued a sombre reminder of the problems that still divide Russia and the West.
He repeated warnings to NATO that Moscow would review relations with the Western defence alliance if it offers membership of ex-Soviet republics.
